title: Nazi Germany and the Holocaust
summary: How Hitler came to power, Nazi racial ideology and propaganda, the persecution of Jews and other groups, the Holocaust, and lessons for human rights today.

notes.text: After World War I, Germany became a democracy called the **Weimar Republic**. It faced economic crises, especially after 1929, when unemployment reached six million. **Adolf Hitler**, leader of the **National Socialist (Nazi) Party**, promised jobs, national pride and to overturn the Treaty of Versailles. In **January 1933** he became Chancellor. Within months he turned Germany into a **dictatorship**.

items: After the Reichstag (parliament) fire in 1933, the **Enabling Act** gave Hitler power to make laws without parliament.
All other political parties and trade unions were banned.
The **Gestapo** (secret police) and the **SS** arrested opponents and sent them to concentration camps.
Joseph Goebbels ran **propaganda**: radio, films, posters and rallies glorified Hitler and spread hatred of Jews.
Books by Jewish and anti-Nazi writers were burned; young people joined the **Hitler Youth**.

notes.title: Why did Germans support the Nazis?
notes.problem: Give two conditions that helped Hitler gain support by 1933.
steps: Economic: the Great Depression brought mass unemployment.
Political: many blamed the Weimar government and resented the Treaty of Versailles, and Nazi propaganda promised to restore Germany.
notes.answer: Economic crisis and resentment of the Treaty of Versailles.

notes.text: The Nazis believed in a false theory of a 'master race' of so-called **Aryans** (white, northern Europeans) and taught that other groups were inferior. They blamed **Jews** for Germany's problems. This **pseudo-science** (false science) about 'race' was used to justify discrimination and murder.
Prejudice, hatred or discrimination against Jewish people.

rows: Boycott of Jewish shops; Jews dismissed from government jobs
**Nuremberg Laws**: Jews lost German citizenship and could not marry non-Jews
**Kristallnacht** ('Night of Broken Glass'): synagogues burned, Jewish shops smashed, about 30 000 Jewish men sent to camps
Jews in occupied Poland forced into overcrowded **ghettos**, such as Warsaw; mobile killing squads shot Jews in the USSR
**Wannsee Conference**: Nazi leaders planned the 'Final Solution', the murder of all Jews in Europe
**Extermination camps** such as Auschwitz-Birkenau and Treblinka; most victims were murdered in gas chambers on arrival

notes.caption: Persecution grew step by step, from boycotts and laws to mass murder.

notes.title: Ordering the steps
notes.problem: Put these in order: Kristallnacht; Nuremberg Laws; boycott of Jewish shops; ghettos in occupied Poland.
notes.answer: Persecution increased step by step, from exclusion to violence.

notes.text: The systematic, state-organised murder of about **six million Jews** by Nazi Germany and its collaborators between 1941 and 1945.

Other groups were also persecuted and murdered: **Roma and Sinti** people, people with disabilities, Polish and Soviet civilians and prisoners of war, gay men, Jehovah's Witnesses and political opponents.
Acts committed with the intention of destroying, in whole or in part, a national, ethnic, racial or religious group.

items: Jewish fighters rose up in the **Warsaw Ghetto Uprising** (1943).
Some non-Jews risked their lives to hide or rescue Jews, for example **Oskar Schindler**, who saved about 1 200 workers. Such people are honoured as the 'Righteous Among the Nations'.
The young German students of the **White Rose** group distributed leaflets against the Nazis and were executed.

notes.title: Source F: Words attributed to Pastor Martin Niemöller (adapted)
notes.text:
First they came for the communists, and I did not speak out, because I was not a communist.
Then they came for the trade unionists, and I did not speak out, because I was not a trade unionist.
Then they came for the Jews, and I did not speak out, because I was not a Jew.
Then they came for me, and there was no one left to speak for me.

notes.label: Lessons for today
notes.text: The Holocaust shows where racism, propaganda and the loss of human rights can lead. After the war, Nazi leaders were tried at the **Nuremberg Trials** for crimes against humanity, and the UN adopted the **Universal Declaration of Human Rights** (1948). South Africa's Constitution also protects human dignity and equality. The Cape Town, Durban and Johannesburg Holocaust & Genocide Centres teach these lessons.
